implementation_notes: Core Data is the write-behind unit of work on Apple platforms: a context registers fetched and inserted objects, tracks property changes, and keeps everything in memory - insertedObjects, updatedObjects and deletedObjects are the pending change set - until save() commits it through the parent context or the persistent store coordinator. Coalescing is automatic (repeated edits before save produce one UPDATE), so what replaces the classic structure is the framework's change tracking plus its save boundary. Use a private-queue context for background flushes and merge into the UI context deliberately.
pitfalls: A context is queue-confined: touching its objects outside perform corrupts state - pass NSManagedObjectID across queues and re-fetch.
save() merges the whole pending set; a conflict throws and leaves the context dirty unless a mergePolicy is set.
Long-lived contexts with retainsRegisteredObjects grow memory and serve stale rows; reset or recreate them per unit of work.

variants.name: SwiftData ModelContext with save()/transaction()/autosave
variants.implementation_notes: SwiftData rebuilds the same discipline over the newer stack: ModelContext tracks every change to registered models (hasChanges, changedModelsArray, insertedModelsArray), keeps them in memory until save() or transaction() writes the pending set to disk, and can autosave on framework events through autosaveEnabled. Choose it for new Swift 5.9+ apps with @Model types; keep Core Data where pre-iOS 17 support, fetched-results controllers, or fine-grained merge policies are required.
pitfalls: Autosave makes the flush boundary implicit: a crash between autosaves loses the window, and tests must disable it to stay deterministic.
A ModelContext is not Sendable - confine it to one actor or create one per task instead of sharing it across threads.
rollback() discards every pending insert/update/delete in the context, so partial undo requires staging work in separate contexts.
